questions.text: Introduce yourself, focusing on aspects not mentioned in your resume.
Explain your project.
Do you have any issues with relocation?
Why should we hire you?

tips.text: Practicing aptitude questions from IndiaBix and GeeksforGeeks (GFG) is sufficient. Just remember the patterns and formulas to solve similar types of problems.
These patterns are repetitive in every Online Assessment, just presented in different forms.
For Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA), start practicing as soon as possible.
When you enter the room, greet them with a smile and a handshake.
Give your introduction confidently because the first impression is the last impression.
You should know the in-depth meaning of every word on your resume. It's not about the number of technologies you list, but how well you know them.

There are standard questions asked about projects, such as: how you would handle a large amount of data, how you would scale the system, why you used a specific technology, and how you would improve performance.
You are the driver of the interview, so the conversation will likely follow the direction you set with your answers.
If there are two interviewers, try to maintain eye contact with both. Keep a smile on your face to show confidence.
They often prioritize motivation and a positive mindset over just technical expertise.
Ask for their names at the end if they didn't introduce themselves at the beginning.
Try to improve your English fluency. Try to speak confidently, even if you make a few grammatical mistakes.
Always smile during the interview.
I feel that the HR interview is about engaging the interviewers with your communication skills, like telling a story about your projects and your learnings. Don't dive deep into technical terms.
Try to show them what a good team player you are.
Confidence, a smile, and honesty are the keys to succeeding in the HR interview.
Don't take the placement process lightly.
Prepare well for placements, especially for the Online Assessment. For DSA, I recommend following only one resource instead of multiple.
Have at least 1-2 strong projects; it's fine if your other projects are simpler.

tips.text: For the Online Assessments, I would suggest doing timed practice of aptitude questions and coding questions too. Be sure to practice CodeForces questions as their style (the way they accept inputs and return outputs) can be quite different from LeetCode questions.
Be confident and explain everything clearly. To explain your projects in detail without going on for too long, preferably use an established method like the STAR method.

If you don’t know something, DO NOT go on a long-winded, vague explanation in hopes that it will be correct. Just say you don’t know it, or you have done it, but forgotten, and the interviewers will move on to the next question.

The above point also applies to answers you are unsure about. Be confident and stick with some answer. Interviewers test your conviction and willpower, they don’t expect you to know everything they ask anyway.
Know your resume in and out. Explain your projects properly and clearly, without sounding too vague. Do not fake anything in it.

When explaining your DSA question’s solution, state and explain your thought process as if it were a tutorial of some sort, rather than going silent completely. Start with the brute force-approach and then provide an optimised solution if prompted.

Be attentive during the pre-placement talk. Take notes if need be. You MUST remain familiar with what the company does, their values, and what they expect from the average applicant, be it technical skills or soft skills.
Work on your communication skills. Even if you have good knowledge, how you convey it might make the difference. Take part in mock interviews and mock speeches to reduce nervousness.

Using all of these for preparation as early as possible is important. Start at most 6 months before the placement period begins. Ensure you know every single programming language and framework on your resume as much as possible.

Add good projects to your resumes. Ones that solve real-world problems, and are innovative and unique. Ensure they are uploaded to your Github account or, even better, deployed on a public URL. Doing an internship before the placement period is also recommended.

tips.text: Actively participating in activities during PPT showcases confidence, helps during the HR rounds, and leave a positive impression on the recruiters.
Ask relevant doubts and clarifying queries during the PPT, as it demonstrates genuine interest in the company and further strengthens your impression.
Start practicing aptitude questions well before placements, as most companies include them in their selection process.
Regularly practice Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA) to handle coding sections efficiently.
Maintain a Good CGPA: Keep your CGPA above 7.5–8, as it helps meet eligibility criteria and creates a strong first impression.

Use a standard, professional template (e.g., Overleaf Resume Template). Make it ATS-friendly; check your score on Resumeworded (aim for 60+). Be truthful—only include skills, projects, and achievements you can confidently discuss. Prepare 4–5 points for each.

Understand the company's work, culture, and role requirements. Prepare relevant questions to ask the interviewer—it shows interest and preparation. Read the job description carefully and incorporate keywords into your answers.
Prepare for standard HR questions in advance to stay confident. Keep answers authentic and personal; avoid over-reliance on AI for this.

Focus on understanding questions thoroughly rather than just solving many. Solve standard problems first; daily practice on platforms like LeetCode or GeeksforGeeks helps. Participate in contests to improve time management, an essential skill for coding rounds. Always check constraints; write brute-force solutions first if optimal solutions are not obvious.
Prioritize important subjects like DBMS and CCN—often asked in technical interviews. Choose open electives wisely (e.g., DBMS) to strengthen placement-related knowledge.
Master your primary language's basics. Be confident discussing syntax, concepts, and memory management. Practice explaining your approach during coding rounds; interviewers often guide you if stuck.
Collaborate with peers with similar goals. Motivate each other, take progress follow-ups, and push to stay on track.
Treat rejections as learning opportunities. Focus on areas you can improve. Placement success also involves timing and luck, stay confident and persistent.

Develop puzzle-solving and critical thinking through platforms like GeeksforGeeks. Practice guesstimates to improve analytical reasoning. Participate in mock interviews to enhance confidence, communication, and interview stamina

tips.text: Be Confident with DSA & SQL : These are the backbone of most technical interviews. Revise key concepts, patterns, and practice problem-solving regularly.
Know Your Resume Inside-Out : Be absolutely clear about every project, internship, and skill mentioned. Don’t lie or exaggerate—be real and authentic.
Present Yourself Confidently : Communication matters as much as technical knowledge. Speak clearly, structure your answers, and show enthusiasm.

Be Mentally Ready for Rejections : Rejections are part of the journey. Before this interview, I had already faced 3 HR round rejections. Each rejection is just redirection—learn from it and keep moving forward.
Keep Applying & Keep Fighting : Consistency is the key. Don’t let one rejection stop you from trying for the next opportunity.
Know the Company : Read about the company’s services, products, and culture. A few lines showing genuine interest can create a positive impression.
Stay Calm in Puzzles & HR Questions : HR and puzzles are often about testing your attitude, logical thinking, and composure—don’t rush, just stay logical and calm.

tips.text: DSA: Easy to medium level is enough for moderate companies. Companies like PhonePe may ask graphs, trees, DP, and advanced problems.
SQL: Asked in almost every interview — know all commands, query execution, differences, and internal workings.
In SQL editors, you can test and debug queries, but in interviews, you won’t have that. Practice writing queries on pen and paper and predicting outputs carefully.
Communication: It’s not just about what you know, but how you answer. Maintain eye contact, stay confident, and avoid pauses or stammering.
OOPs: Prepare in detail with real-life examples and references to your projects/code.
Core Subjects: Basics of OS, DBMS, and Computer Networks are usually sufficient.
System Design: Asked only in specific companies like IDFC, not everywhere.
Know your projects thoroughly — tech stack, challenges faced, standout features, and future improvements.
Be ready to explain why you chose the project and why that tech stack.
Prepare basic HR questions (strengths, weaknesses, goals) and practice puzzles from GeeksforGeeks (GFG).
